books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Presidential election results, November 4, 1856. Figures from the American Presidency Project (presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/elections/1856); 296 electoral votes in all, 149 needed to win. Fillmore carried only Maryland.
stimulus.text:
| Candidate | Party | Popular votes | Share | Electoral votes |
| James Buchanan | Democratic | 1,836,072 | 45.3% | 174 |
| John C. Frémont | Republican | 1,342,345 | 33.1% | 114 |
| Millard Fillmore | American (Know-Nothing) | 873,053 | 21.5% | 8 |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to the table, the winner of the 1856 election was

options.text: John C. Frémont, the Republican candidate.
options.misconception: Frémont ran second with 114 electoral votes, not first.
Fillmore carried only Maryland, for 8 electoral votes.

options.text: William L. Dayton, the Republican for vice president.
options.misconception: Dayton ran for vice president beside Frémont, and the ticket lost.

rationales.A: Frémont ran second with 114 electoral votes, not first.
rationales.B: Fillmore carried only Maryland, for 8 electoral votes.
rationales.C: Dayton ran for vice president beside Frémont, and the ticket lost.
rationales.D: The table gives Buchanan 174 electoral votes and 45.3 percent of the popular vote, the most of any candidate.
rationales.general:
1. Read the electoral column: Buchanan 174, Frémont 114, Fillmore 8.
2. Read the popular column: Buchanan 45.3 percent, Frémont 33.1, Fillmore 21.5.
3. Name the winner: the Democrat, with a plurality of the people and a majority of the electors.
4. Check the map: Frémont won eleven free states and no slave state, so the vote was sectional.
Remember: in a three-way race, read both columns; the people’s choice and the electors’ choice can differ.
